text_blocks.snippet: The history of fluoride in public health began with observations of mottled, yet cavity-resistant teeth in areas with naturally high fluoride levels. Dentist Frederick McKay's research in the early 1900s led to the discovery that "Colorado brown stain" was caused by fluoride in the water supply. Further research demonstrated that a lower, safe level of fluoride could reduce tooth decay, leading to the implementation of water fluoridation programs, starting with Grand Rapids, Michigan in the 1940s.

list.title: Early Observations:
list.snippet: In the early 20th century, dentists like Frederick McKay noticed a peculiar condition called "Colorado brown stain" in some communities. This stain, now known as dental fluorosis, was caused by excessive fluoride in the water. However, McKay also observed that these individuals had remarkably low rates of tooth decay.
